statement: In people who use cannabis, using cannabis of higher strength, as each study defined it (stronger herbal types such as skunk or sinsemilla, types of 10% THC or more, hash in one survey, liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample, or concentrates), compared with lower-strength cannabis, is associated with more signs of cannabis use disorder in four of the six studies found by a systematic review searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022), all of them cross-sectional, one rated fair and five poor. In a UK online drug survey of 2,514 people, each extra day a month of using skunk went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.25 points higher (scale 0 to 15, 3 or more taken to indicate dependence; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.36), with no association for grass or resin (adjusted for age and gender); in a survey of 55,240 people from 175 countries, the groups using sinsemilla or hashish alongside herbal cannabis scored 0.16 and 0.26 points higher than the group using herbal cannabis only (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added); in a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, people who used stronger cannabis were more likely to report recent cannabis problems on a screening test (adjusted odds ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.41 to 11.81, adjusted for frequency of use, age at first use, sex and childhood socio-economic position); and among 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, people who used liquid or resin forms more often had a dependence syndrome than people who used dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 6.85, 95% CI 1.87 to 25.15 in the table, 1.19 to 25.15 in the text; no adjustment listed). The two studies that compared concentrates with herbal cannabis found no clear difference: in 156 US adults, neither concentrate nor stronger herbal use was associated with use-disorder symptoms (the interval printed for concentrates does not contain its own estimate), and in 191 US adults, people who frequently used concentrates did not report significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3, with few symptoms overall). Every study relied on what people said they used; none measured THC in their cannabis or how much they took in, only one adjusted for the amount used, and no study followed people over time or compared them with people who do not use cannabis. The review's Discussion says higher-strength use was "consistently associated with an increased risk of CUD", which is stronger than these results. Its senior author is an author of three of the four studies that found an association (the two surveys and the UK sample, which another review author led); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no clear difference are by other groups. A later narrative review (Inman & Cservenka, online 2024; 27 articles found through PubMed and citation searches, not appraised) says that studies have consistently linked concentrate use with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms, citing mainly the survey of 191 people as showing more symptoms, together with US college and web surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates; it does not cite the systematic review. It finds little information on cannabis use disorder with edibles and argues only by analogy with slower-acting forms of other drugs, and concludes that how often people use cannabis remains the most reliable predictor across all forms and that a causal role of strength is not established. As a base rate, a meta-analysis of 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (Leung et al., 2020; studies published 2009 to 2020, over half from the US, mostly DSM-IV) puts the share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria for cannabis use disorder at 22 in 100 (95% CI 18 to 26) and for dependence at 13 in 100 (10 to 15), pooling lifetime, past-year and past-month measures, with single studies ranging from 4.5 in 100 (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41 in 100 (21-year-olds in one Australian cohort); dependence was 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people who used weekly or daily, against 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. That review found no population study that estimated the risk by the strength of the cannabis used, and it did not appraise the studies it pooled. Funding as printed: the systematic review, an Economic and Social Research Council doctoral studentship, Cancer Research UK fellowship and project awards and a Wellcome Trust grant (funder without a role), with one author reporting previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and a consulting company doing unrelated work; the narrative review, no funding and no conflicts; the meta-analysis, University of Queensland and NHMRC fellowships and Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding of the authors' centre, with no conflicts. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Some studies asked people which kind of cannabis they mostly used and checked for signs of cannabis use disorder, when cannabis use gets hard to control and causes problems. In four of six such studies, people who used cannabis with more THC, such as skunk, had more signs of the disorder; the two studies that compared concentrates (strong extracts such as wax or shatter) with plant cannabis found no clear difference. All six asked people only once, relied on what they said they used and did not measure THC, so they cannot show that stronger cannabis causes the disorder. A later review says concentrates are linked to more problems, but it leans mostly on one of those two studies; it says little is known yet about edibles, and that how often people use cannabis is the most reliable sign of risk. For comparison, large surveys in richer countries found that about 22 in 100 people who had used cannabis had a cannabis use disorder, and about 13 in 100 were dependent; none of those surveys looked at how strong the cannabis was.
population: People who use cannabis: respondents to online drug surveys (UK, n = 2,514; 175 countries, n = 55,240), a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24, US convenience samples of 156 and 191 adults, and 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (Petrilli 2022, six cross-sectional studies); US surveys of college students, high-school students, adults and web samples (Inman 2026, narrative review); and, for the base rate, people who had ever, recently or regularly used cannabis in 21 general-population studies from the US, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland and France (Leung 2020).
exposure: Self-reported use of higher-strength cannabis as each study defined it: skunk, sinsemilla or other stronger herbal types; types typically of 10% THC or more; hash classed with stronger types in one survey; liquid or resin forms in one clinical sample; concentrates (including butane hash oil) in the two US samples and the narrative review, which also compares flower and edibles as forms. Strength bands are study definitions only. For the base rate, any cannabis use (ever, past year or month, or weekly or daily).
comparator: Lower-strength cannabis as each study defined it (grass, resin or herbal types; types typically under 10% THC; dry herbal cannabis); in the two concentrate studies, people who use herbal cannabis (frequently, in one). No study compared with people who do not use cannabis. For the base rate, none (a share of people who had used cannabis).
outcome: Signs of cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale scores (0 to 15; 3 or more taken to indicate dependence), recent problems on the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test, a MINI cannabis screening test, a self-report symptom questionnaire, or ICD-10 dependence syndrome by clinical interview; for the base rate, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV (abuse or dependence) or DSM-5 cannabis use disorder from structured interviews.
magnitude: Systematic review (Petrilli 2022), six cross-sectional studies, higher against lower strength: Severity of Dependence Scale b 0.254 (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357) per extra day a month of skunk use, grass 0.020 (-0.029 to 0.070), resin 0.025 (-0.019 to 0.067) (UK survey, 2,514; poor); b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209) for sinsemilla with herbal and 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337) for hashish with herbal against herbal only (175-country survey, 55,240; poor); recent problems, adjusted odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81) (UK sample, 1,087; fair); dependence syndrome, odds ratio 6.85 (1.87 to 25.15 in Table 2; 1.19 to 25.15 in the text) for liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis (71 Japanese patients; poor); no association in 156 US adults (stronger herbal r 0.09, -0.12 to 0.30; concentrates -0.05, interval printed as -0.35 to -0.26; poor); no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use in 191 US adults (mean symptoms 2.1 against 1.3; poor). Narrative review (Inman 2026): no effect sizes. Base rate (Leung 2020; 21 studies, 153 data points, high-income countries): cannabis use disorder 22 in 100 (18 to 26), abuse 13 in 100 (8 to 18), dependence 13 in 100 (10 to 15) among people who had used cannabis; use disorder by design and recall period, 17 in 100 (12 to 23) to 28 in 100 (10 to 48); dependence with weekly or daily use 33 in 100 (22 to 44) in two cohorts of young people and 18 in 100 (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies; single studies from 4.5 in 100 (use disorder, US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1 in 100 (lifetime use disorder, Australian 21-year-olds). No estimate by strength or form exists in these sources.

evidence.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 736-737); Results, 1st and 10th paragraphs (pp. 737, 744); Table 2 (pp. 741-742)
evidence.extracted: Systematic review of observational studies (MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO to 14 January 2021; PROSPERO CRD42021226447) comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it. Six cross-sectional studies examined cannabis use disorder: one rated fair and five poor on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, for limits in the measure of exposure in all six and in outcome measures, sample selection and confounder adjustment in the poor ones. Exposure was self-reported in all six. Outcomes: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample of 1,087), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156) and an ICD-10 clinical interview (71 Japanese patients).

UK online survey 2009-10 (2,514; skunk against grass and resin; adjusted for gender and age; poor): each extra day a month of higher-potency use went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.254 higher (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357 in Table 2; 0.161 to 0.3578 in the text), with no association for grass (0.020, -0.029 to 0.070) or resin (0.025, -0.019 to 0.067). Survey of 55,240 people in 175 countries 2017-18 (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added; poor): the classes using sinsemilla and herbal (b 0.155, 0.100 to 0.209) and hashish and herbal (b 0.262, 0.188 to 0.337) scored higher than the class using herbal only. UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (Cannabis Abuse Screening Test; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, age at first use and frequency; fair): recent cannabis problems with higher-potency use, odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (ICD-10 interview; no adjustment listed; poor): liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145 in Table 2; 6.9, 1.19 to 25.15, in the text).

US sample of 156 people (self-report questionnaire; no adjustment listed; poor): higher-potency herbal use and use-disorder symptoms r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30); for concentrates the review prints -0.05 (-0.35 to -0.26), an interval that does not contain its own estimate, and the text reads it as fewer symptoms. US sample of 191 (MINI cannabis screening test; no adjustment listed; poor): people who frequently used concentrates did not endorse significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3); the review notes that the sample endorsed few symptoms overall. These are the only two studies in the review that compare concentrates with herbal cannabis on cannabis use disorder.

The Discussion states that higher-potency use was consistently associated with an increased risk of cannabis use disorder, recent problems and dependence severity, citing animal self-administration studies and an association of rising potency with treatment entry. The limits it states: self-reported product type as a proxy for THC, THC intake not measured (titration expected to weaken associations), cross-sectional designs that cannot establish direction, no agreement on confounders, and amount used adjusted for in only one study. The Conclusion draws recommendations for education, clinical management and regulation by THC concentration from these findings, without a certainty rating.

evidence.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)
evidence.extracted: Funding: ESRC doctoral studentship (KP), Cancer Research UK fellowship and project award (GT), Wellcome Trust (LH); the funder had no role. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a consulting company doing unrelated work; the others declare none. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of three of the four cannabis use disorder studies that found an association (the 2015 UK survey, the 2020 175-country survey and the 2020 UK sample, of which review author L Hines is first author); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no clear difference are by other groups.

evidence.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates › CUD outcomes, paragraph; references 37, 40, 42 and 43 (p. 12)
evidence.extracted: The review states that concentrate use has been consistently associated with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018, the US sample of 191 that the systematic review reports as showing no significant difference); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, a 2021 review); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). It gives no effect sizes and calls for longitudinal studies.

evidence.locator: Results › Cannabis flower › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 6); Discussion › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 9)
evidence.extracted: The review calls the literature on problematic use by form small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and cannabis use disorder risk (ref. 52), more symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more cannabis use disorder with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it says, without a citation, that inhaling is generally linked to a higher risk than swallowing. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of cannabis use disorder risk across all forms and that further causal factors such as quantity and THC potency are yet to be firmly established. For flower, it cites a survey of 617 Colorado college students in which flower potency was positively associated with symptom count and severity (ref. 36), and says flower's outcomes have rarely been compared with other forms.

evidence.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles › CUD outcomes, paragraph; Results › Cannabis edibles › Conclusion, paragraph
evidence.extracted: There is limited information specific to the cannabis use disorder potential of edibles. The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often naming edibles as their main form. It concludes that the cannabis use disorder outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.

evidence.locator: Abstract and Highlights (p. 3); Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 4-5); Figure 1 (p. 4); Disclosure statement and Funding (p. 10)
evidence.extracted: Narrative review: PubMed keyword searches screened by title and abstract for relevance; 4,077 articles found, 216 reviewed, 20 included and 7 added from reference lists and citing articles, 27 in all; no dates, criteria beyond relevance or appraisal of the included studies are stated; the authors scored their own review 12 of 12 on SANRA. The 72 references do not include the 2022 systematic review (editors' check). The Abstract says concentrate use may be associated with a greater cannabis use disorder risk and that form-specific longitudinal data are lacking; the Highlights state the association without a hedge. No funding; no conflicts reported. Published online 26 October 2024.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 2); Results › Meta-analysis results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 11); Table 2 (p. 28)
evidence.extracted: Random-effects pooled shares among people in general-population samples who had used cannabis: cannabis use disorder 22% (95% CI 18 to 26), abuse 13% (8 to 18), dependence 13% (10 to 15). Use disorder by design and recall period: cohorts, lifetime use 27% (25 to 28) and recent use 22% (20 to 24); cross-sectional, lifetime 28% (10 to 48), past year or month 17% (12 to 23), weekly or daily 22% (17 to 28). Dependence: cohorts, lifetime 12% (7 to 18), recent 9% (1 to 19), weekly or daily 33% (22 to 44); cross-sectional, lifetime 11% (7 to 15), recent 8% (6 to 10), daily or near daily 18% (12 to 24). The three pools draw on different sets of studies (255,010, 28,951 and 58,661 observations), so they cannot be added or compared directly.

evidence.locator: Method › Protocol; Selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Search strategy; Analysis, 2nd paragraph (pp. 5-7); Results › Study selection, paragraph; Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: PROSPERO CRD42019133166. General-population observational studies with DSM or ICD diagnoses from structured interviews; prisoners and other high-risk or sub-populations excluded; studies published from 2009 (PubMed for cohorts and Global Burden of Disease data sources for surveys, February 2019, updated April 2020). 1,383 records, 130 full texts, 21 studies, 153 data points (several per study, by sex, age, survey year or recall period). Samples from the US, the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 15 studies gave cross-sectional and 9 longitudinal data; 11 sampled adolescents or young adults. Nine counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required use more than a few times, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use. One study used DSM-III-R and one DSM-5, the rest DSM-IV, in which use disorder means abuse or dependence; separate analyses by DSM version were planned but are not reported. No appraisal of the included studies is reported.

evidence.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 4th to 6th paragraphs (pp. 9-10); Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 12-13)
evidence.extracted: Single-study estimates: use disorder from 4.5% (1.8 to 7.3) in US adults aged 50 or more who used in the past year (2005-06) to 41.1% (38.4 to 43.8), lifetime, in an Australian cohort of 21-year-olds; abuse from 2.9% to 28.4%; dependence from 3.5% (0.1 to 7.0) in young adults in Ireland to 40.9% (29.0 to 52.8) among people using daily in an Australian adolescent cohort; past-year dependence 14.7% (13.0 to 16.5) among US adults using daily or near daily in 2017. The 33% (22 to 44) for weekly or daily use comes from two longitudinal studies of young people (Australia and the Netherlands); cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18% (12 to 24). In one US study, dependence was 10.6% (7.1 to 14.1) among everyone who had ever used and 18.1% (12.4 to 23.8) among those who had used more than six times.

The authors found no population study that estimated the risk of cannabis use disorder by the potency of the products used, and mention, without a reference, a Michigan study of high-risk families in which people who used higher-potency products had higher risks of developing use-disorder symptoms. Limits they state: heterogeneity, with limited power to detect moderators; 60% of estimates from cross-sectional surveys open to recall bias; lifetime and past-year estimates that differ in meaning (past-year use disorder 15.4% among 18 to 25-year-olds who used that year against 9.8% among those who had ever used, in one US survey); all studies from high-income countries, over half from the US.

evidence.locator: Role of Funding Sources; Contributors; Conflict of Interest
evidence.extracted: University of Queensland development fellowship (JL); NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (LH); the authors' centre and group (Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research; Lives Lived Well) supported by Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding; the funding bodies had no role. All authors declare no conflicts of interest.

risk_of_bias.note: Petrilli 2022 (AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional) rates five of the six cannabis use disorder studies poor and one fair: self-reported product type as the exposure, cross-sectional designs, self-selected online or convenience samples and a clinical sample, confounder adjustment ranging from none to frequency and amount, and no measure of THC intake. Inman 2026 is a narrative review rated high risk on the editors' checklist. Leung 2020 (AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional) did not appraise the surveys it pooled.

inconsistency.note: Four studies find more signs of the disorder with higher strength and two find no clear difference; the two null studies are the only direct comparisons of concentrates with herbal cannabis, and the two reviews describe one of them differently (no significant difference against more symptoms). The direction is otherwise consistent.

indirectness.note: Strength is inferred from self-reported product type, not measured THC or THC intake; four of the six outcomes are screening or severity scales rather than diagnoses; the samples are online, convenience or clinical; and the base rate comes from general-population surveys in high-income countries that did not measure strength or form.

imprecision.note: The two large surveys give narrow intervals; the smaller studies' wide intervals (1.41 to 11.81; 1.87 to 25.15) are reported. Not downgraded further: the certainty is already at its floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: no meta-analysis of strength and cannabis use disorder, and the systematic review did not examine it.

dose_response.note: The per-day gradient in one survey concerns how often stronger cannabis is used, not strength itself, and comes from a poor-quality cross-sectional study.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: cross-sectional studies with self-reported exposure, five of six rated poor, adjustment ranging from none to frequency and amount, and a narrative review and a pooled prevalence without appraisal. Inconsistency -1: two of six studies, the only direct comparisons of concentrates with herbal cannabis, find no clear difference, and the two reviews disagree on one of them. Indirectness -1: product type as a proxy for THC, screening scales for four of six outcomes, selected samples, and a base rate not split by strength. These downgrades pass the floor, so the certainty is very low. Not downgraded for imprecision or publication bias, and no upgrade (the one gradient mixes strength with frequency of use). Overlapping evidence: three of the four studies that found an association share an author with the review and two of them are described as annual drug surveys, so they are not fully independent replications. Worded 'is associated with' because no study can show direction. The base rate (Leung 2020) is given as a description of the populations sampled; as a description it rests on unappraised surveys pooled across recall periods and DSM versions and would itself be rated low at best.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice; strengths and THC bands appear only as study definitions. Split from cl_can_concentrates as the batch 10 brief allows: dependence by strength and form is a different outcome and body of evidence from that claim's acute comparison of concentrates with flower. Rests on one systematic review without meta-analysis (Petrilli 2022: AMSTAR 2 low confidence, provisional, appendix not read), one narrative review (Inman 2026: editors' checklist high) and one meta-analysis of prevalence used as the base rate (Leung 2020: AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional; read from the journal pre-proof, supplements S1 to S6 not read). All anchors are ai-located by AI reader 93 and need a second reader. The six primary studies (Freeman & Winstock 2015; Craft et al. 2020; Hines et al. 2020; Matsumoto et al. 2020; Prince & Conner 2019; Bidwell et al. 2018) were not read and have no reference records; their figures are as Petrilli reports them, and Petrilli's text and tables disagree on two of them. The two reviews describe Bidwell et al. 2018 (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004) differently; reading it would settle that. Three of the four studies that found an association share an author with Petrilli 2022: a reason to read closely, not to discount. The Leung anchors could later move to a section 8 base-rate claim on cannabis use disorder (editor's choice).
